name: Probiotics for acne

lead: Probiotics are live bacteria sold as capsules, fermented foods and skin products. Acne-prone people use them hoping for less inflammation and fewer breakouts.

The proposed routes are the gut-skin axis, where gut microbes influence inflammation and hormones, and shifts in skin bacteria such as C. acnes. A lab study found skin S. epidermidis can inhibit C. acnes through fermentation. Several meta-analyses of randomised trials appeared in 2025, and reviews describe the findings as preliminary, with early signs of fewer inflammatory lesions and better skin barrier function.

paras: People take oral probiotic capsules or eat fermented foods daily, or apply topical products to the face, usually alongside a regular skincare routine. Benefits reported in studies are strain-specific, so results do not carry over between products. Users typically allow several weeks before judging skin.

Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in immunocompromised or critically ill people, who have reason to avoid them. Effects depend on the strain, and regulators such as EFSA have rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.

angle.text: Acne-prone users take oral probiotics or use topical ones to shift gut or skin microbes, lowering inflammation and breakouts. Reviews and trials exist, with results that vary by strain.

lead: Probiotics are live microorganisms intended to confer a health benefit, sold as supplements, in fermented foods and in some topical products [1]. For acne, oral and topical probiotics are discussed on the basis of the proposed gut-skin axis and of the skin's own microbial community [2][3].

Published reviews describe the research as preliminary. A review summarised in Wikipedia describes probiotics and synbiotics as showing early potential to reduce inflammatory acne lesions and improve skin barrier function [1]. Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials of oral probiotics were published in 2025 [4][5][6]. Benefits of probiotics are generally strain-specific, so results do not transfer between products [1].
infobox: Gut-skin axis; skin microbiome modulation; reduced inflammation
Dietary supplements (US); EU bans the word on labels [1]

paras: Acne involves abnormal keratinisation of the sebaceous duct, colonisation by Cutibacterium acnes, raised sebum production and hormonal factors, and treatment can be long and affect quality of life [3]. Researchers have proposed that the gut microbiota influences these processes, which is the basis for oral probiotic use [3].

Laboratory work has also examined the skin microbiome. A 2014 study reported that Staphylococcus epidermidis can ferment glycerol in ways that inhibit growth of C. acnes, and suggested implications for probiotic treatment [7]. Reviews of the cutaneous microbiota describe dysbiosis as contributing to acne [8]. Diet is another suspected influence, and a 2021 review discusses glycemic load and acne [9].

A scoping review (2025) examined probiotic supplements and topical applications for acne [10], a 2013 article reviewed probiotics in acne and rosacea [2], and a 2022 narrative review covered the microbiome and probiotics in acne vulgaris [3]. Meta-analyses of randomised trials of oral probiotics were published in 2025 in Cureus, Medicina and Clinical and Experimental Dermatology [4][5][6]; their individual findings are not summarised here.

Trial registrations show a range of designs: an oral probiotic added to benzoyl peroxide plus adapalene (n=400, phase 4) [11], probiotics compared with azithromycin (n=75) and combined with azithromycin (n=60) [12][13], a topical probiotic cream study (n=20) [14], and trials of oral probiotics against placebo in patients with moderate acne [15][16]. A trial of probiotics and skin hydration in youth with mild acne has been completed [17]. Registration entries do not report outcomes in the material reviewed.

Probiotics are generally considered safe, but immunocompromised people, premature infants and people with central venous catheters or heart valve disease may face higher risks, and bloodstream infections have been rarely reported [1]. The European Food Safety Authority has rejected commercial probiotic health claim petitions for insufficient evidence, and the US FDA and FTC have issued warning letters over disease claims [1].
A 2026 study reported on Lactobacillus-derived extracellular vesicles as a multi-target acne approach in laboratory research [18].

timeline.event: Review article on probiotics in acne and rosacea published in Cutis [2].
Study reports S. epidermidis fermentation inhibiting C. acnes, with probiotic implications [7].
